title: From 36% to 59%: How EU Private Label Share Varies and What It Means for Your Brand
summary: Private label unit share ranges from 36% in Italy to 59% in Spain. Here is how that variation shapes the opportunity for branded suppliers across EU grocery markets.
body_markdown:
**In this article, learn about:**


- Why the European average for private label hides very different conditions in each country


- Which EU markets give branded products more room to compete


- Which product categories give brands a strong position across all markets


- How to decide where to focus your EU retail relationships


## One Number, Many Different Realities


Private label crossed 50% of grocery unit sales across Europe's six biggest markets in 2026.[Circana's analysis](https://www.circana.com/post/private-label-reaches-record-50-unit-share-across-europe-s-six-biggest-grocery-markets) covers France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and the UK. By value, private label is worth €324bn across those markets, at 42% of grocery spend.


That 50% figure has been climbing every year since 2021. What it does not show is which markets that number comes from, or how much variation sits behind the average. Spain is at 59% private label unit share. Italy is at 36%. Poland sits around 25%. For a branded supplier deciding where to build EU retail relationships, the country you choose is as important as the category you lead with.


The country you choose shapes the conversation before the buyer meeting even starts.


## The Countries Where Private Label Has the Deepest Roots


**Spain (59%)** has specific reasons for its position. Mercadona holds roughly a quarter of the national grocery market, and its Hacendado and Deliplus own-brand ranges are among the most recognised consumer brands in Spain in their own right. Spanish consumers moved toward private label heavily during the economic crisis of the early 2010s. That buying habit stayed.


**The Netherlands (56%)** is concentrated around Albert Heijn and Jumbo, both of which have invested heavily in their own-brand ranges. Albert Heijn's AH own brand is seen by Dutch shoppers as a quality benchmark. It competes on the same level as national brands across most categories, with strong packaging and product development to match.


**Germany (52%)** has had hard discount as part of its grocery structure for decades. Aldi and Lidl operate at large scale in their home market, with private label ranges that define the format. The main grocery retailers, Rewe and Edeka, have built their own private label ranges in response. Branded products find room here, but the expectation that a branded product costs more than the own-label version is applied across the whole category.


**France (46%)** sits in the middle. Regional food identity and origin-certified products give brands a cultural advantage in some categories. The cooperative retail structure, through networks like E.Leclerc, means buying decisions are not always made in the same way as in a fully centralised retailer.


## Markets Where Brands Have More Room


Italy's food culture is a large part of why the country sits 14 points below the six-market average. Italian grocery retail has more independent and regional retailers than northern European markets, and there is a category of food identity attached to origin-certified products that retailers can't replicate under their own label. Products with a protected designation of origin, such as Parmigiano Reggiano, Prosciutto di Parma, Grana Padano, and Sicilian and Puglian olive oils with DOP status, are defined by geography and production standard. No retailer can put their own brand on them.


For branded food suppliers, particularly in ambient grocery, premium chilled, and specialist categories, Italy is a market where product story and brand equity carry real weight in buyer meetings. Private label is growing there: it rose 4.1% in value in 2025. But the starting position is much lower than in northern Europe, and the cultural factors behind that are not changing quickly. If you are thinking about Italy as a starting point, it helps to understand what EU buyers are asking about origin before you get to the range conversation. We covered that in detail in[EU Buyers Are Asking Where Your Products Come From. Here Is Why.](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/eu-buyers-are-asking-where-your-products-come-from-here-is-why)


Central and Eastern Europe presents a similar opportunity at a market level. Poland and the Czech Republic are markets where branded FMCG still has the shelf space and buyer appetite that western European branded suppliers lost years ago.

## Categories Where Brands Win Regardless of Market


The country shapes how much room branded products have. The category shapes what you can win once you are there.


Premium pet food is one of the clearest examples of a category where brands hold strong.[Private label holds around 75% of economy pet food value in Western Europe but only 4-5% of the premium tier.](https://globalpetindustry.com/article/the-repositioning-of-private-label-pet-food/) Shoppers buying premium cat and dog food make a trust decision. Retailers have built strong own-brand ranges at the economy end; they have made very little progress at the premium end.


Functional food, covering high-protein, high-fibre, and fortified products, is a category where branded products are growing faster than private label right now. That gap will likely close as retailers develop their own functional ranges. Brands with established positions in this space have a window, probably two to three years wide.


Origin and provenance-led products give brands a structural advantage across all markets. Any product with a geographic designation, a certified production method, or a verifiable production story is harder for a retailer to copy. The category leader is defined by the place and the production method, not a logo. Retailers can invest in their own sourcing, but they can't replicate the product's history.


Beverages remain one of the hardest categories for private label to grow. Brand trust and shopper identity are more embedded in drink choices than in ambient food. Where those two things are weaker, in basic water and commodity soft drinks, the dynamics look different. But across beverages broadly, branded products hold.


## Choosing Where to Build Your EU Retail Relationships


There are two decisions that branded suppliers making an EU retail strategy tend to separate, when they should really make them together: which markets to enter, and which categories to lead with.


A branded food range that struggles in the Netherlands, where private label has been a quality standard for years, may find a genuinely open conversation in Italy or Poland. The buyers are different, the competition is different, and the room on the shelf is different. For suppliers considering EU expansion beyond the established western markets, that difference in starting position is worth building into the plan from the beginning.


For suppliers managing EU retail connections through[SPS Commerce](https://www.spscommerce.com/products/fulfillment/) , adding a new market connection, whether that is an Italian grocery retailer or a Polish retail chain, goes through the same SPS network that handles existing retail relationships. The strategy of which markets to enter is the harder question. The connection itself follows from that decision.
